newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean banks to finalise Jinro rescue on Monday.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean banks to finalise Jinro rescue on Monday.

text.p: South Korea's commercial banks are scheduled to meet on Monday to try to put the finishing touches on a bail-out plan for debt-ridden Jinro Group, which has so far escaped becoming the third big bankruptcy this year.
Analysts said the key to the rescue of the nation's 19th largest industrial conglomerate would be a group of merchant banks that has balked at granting fresh loans.
Banks have formed a voluntary committee to keep Jinro and other troubled corporates afloat by deferring debt payments and extending new credit. The committee meets on Monday.
Merchant banks have agreed to accept the committee's decision on deferring debt, but have been adamant they cannot risk pumping fresh capital into shaky enterprises.
Analysts said the committee cannot succeed without them.

"The merchant banks want some skewing of the committee's arrangement in their favor," said Henry Morris, managing director of Coryo International (H.K.) Ltd. "If they don't get it, they could demand repayment from Jinro and proceed through the courts."
Analysts said the government was probably pressuring the merchant banks to compromise and avoid a chain of failures that could shake the economy.
Last week the Finance Ministry announced plans for a 1.5 trillion won ($1.68 billion) fund to take over bad debts among banks and help teetering companies dispose of assets.
Jinro, the country's oldest and largest maker of distilled spirits, is buckling under debts estimated at 3.2 trillion won ($3.58 billion), largely the result of reckless expansion.

With the country still reeling from the collapse of Hanbo Steel Co in January and Sammi Steel Co in March, Jinro's creditors stopped short of pushing Jinro into bankruptcy when the group began to default on debt payments this month.
Commercial banks agreed last Monday to freeze Jinro's debts and keep its credit lines open.
The merhant banks agreed only that they would not call in the stricken company's notes.
The presidents of the top 30 merchant banks, after what local newspapers described as a stormy and heated exchange, decided to stick to their position in a gathering on Thursday.
By the weekend, it looked like that stubbornness would pay off. After a midnight meeting on Friday, commercial banks said they would offer on Monday to exempt merchant banks from new loans.
Merchant banks hold most of the 1.7 trillion won in debts that Jinro owes to non-bank financial institutions, while commercial banks are owed 1.2 trillion won, the Federation of Korean Banks said.
Merchant banks, with smaller capital bases, typically extend loans with little or no collateral.

"It would be difficult for merchant banks to supply fresh credit to Jinro unless commercial banks or the government provide some sort of guarantee," said Koo Kyung-hoi, an analyst at Dongwon Economic Research Institute.
For instance, merchant banks could be assured that a certain part of their loans would be repaid if the committee's rescue of Jinro failed, he said.
Some analysts said the merchant banks would have little choice but to participate in the rescue committee.

"Merchant banks may have to contribute to banks' efforts to save Jinro because the group's collapse could cause a chain reaction of corporate failures," said Yoon Suk-hun, an economist at the Korea Institute of Finance.
